key_insight: Passive wall deformations can either damp or amplify Tollmien–Schlichting waves depending on phase, amplitude, and streamwise placement, enabling localized or downstream stabilization but also a full reversal of the control effect.
engineering_relevance: The work defines practical design limits for passive boundary-layer control and suggests phononic subsurfaces as a route to flow-surface interfaces that suppress instability without active actuation.
method: Compare elastic wall admittance against a rigid-wall baseline
Decompose perturbation-energy budget into work-rate, viscous energy, production, and dissipation
Study how streamwise translation and anisotropic phononic subsurface response change stability outcomes
evidence_signal: The abstract reports a model-based energy analysis and parametric study identifying thresholds where stabilization becomes destabilization, but does not mention experimental or high-fidelity validation data.
watch_item: Passive control is highly sensitive to phase and streamwise location, so small geometric or material mismatches could negate the intended stabilizing effect.
paper_title: A deep dive into Tollmien-Schlichting wave control via passive wall deformations: The battle between local and downstream stabilization, lessons learned, and implications for phononic subsurfaces
